prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I am so lonely for the twentieth century, for the deeply felt, obscene graffiti of armed men and the beautiful bridges that make them so small and carry them into the hearts of cities written like words across nothing, the dense void history became in my beautiful century. When a man talks reason, he postpones something. He gets in the way of a machine that knows him for the sad vengeance he is, somewhere close to the bald name of his city. "New York" means "strike back." "Attica" means "strike back" and so does anyplace in the world in the huge eyes and tender hands of my century. I went to the capital. I had a banner, and there were thousands of people like me. There was an airplane, and for a moment heavy with laurel and sprays of peach blossom something that has never happened before stretched like a woman's shadow on a hedge between the plane and the people who saw it flying. It was the real name of the century. It told everyone to strike back until there was no reason in the world except a machine stalled overhead that knows everyone and is as delicate as peach blossom. But the poor years come too late.

# Longing for a Vanished Century

There is a deep and aching nostalgia that pulls the speaker backward toward the twentieth century—a longing so profound that it transforms even the era's brutalities into objects of romantic devotion. The violence of those decades, the graffiti scrawled across urban walls, the towering bridges that spanned rivers and connected worlds: all of these are remembered not with horror but with reverence, as though the century's harshness carried within it a kind of terrible beauty now lost to time.

Against this backdrop, rational discourse appears not as a solution but as an impediment. Reasoned argument and careful deliberation seem only to delay what the speaker senses is unavoidable—a mechanized, almost industrial confrontation with the accumulated sorrow and desire for vengeance that lies beneath the surface of human life. Logic postpones the reckoning, but it cannot prevent it; beneath every measured word waits an inevitable settling of accounts.

In this vision, the names of cities become something larger than geography. "New York" and "Attica" cease to be mere locations and instead ring out as universal summonses, cries to "strike back" that echo across the globe. They embody a shared spirit of resistance, a rebellion that belongs to no single place but to all who have felt the weight of injustice and the impulse to rise against it.

The speaker then turns to memory, recalling a day spent among thousands of protesters gathered in the capital. In that crowd, an airplane passing overhead and a brief, flickering vision seemed—if only for an instant—to crystallize the true meaning of the century itself. In that fleeting moment, amid the mass of bodies and voices, something essential became visible, a truth that the rest of the age had only gestured toward.

Yet the poem does not end in triumph or clarity. Instead, it closes on a note of melancholy and futility. Whatever meaning or transformation the speaker sought, it seems to arrive only after the moment for it has passed. Understanding comes too late; change, if it comes at all, appears when it can no longer matter. The century recedes, and with it the possibility of grasping what it might have meant.
outputs.L4:
# The Century That Struck Back

We were born into machinery. The gears turned before we opened our eyes, and by the time we learned to speak, the language we inherited was already fluent in steel and smoke. This is the century that made us and unmade us, over and over, until we could no longer distinguish the difference.

*Strike back*, the pavement whispered beneath a thousand marching feet.

*Strike back*, the factory windows shivered, catching light like broken teeth.

I remember the airplanes most of all—not for where they carried us, but for how they made the sky into something owned, something crossed and recrossed by silver bodies that hummed with indifference. We watched them from below, small in our upturned faces, and felt the old ache: to rise, to leave, to become as weightless as the exhaust trails dissolving into blue. But we were rooted. We were the ground they flew above.

*Strike back*, said the mother whose son did not return.

*Strike back*, said the placard, the pamphlet, the fist raised in the square.

The cities grew around us like coral, accreting layer upon layer of glass and desire. Neon bled into the puddles. Somewhere a siren rehearsed its single desperate note, and we mistook it, sometimes, for music. We were so many, pressed together in the subway cars, in the bread lines, in the crowds that gathered and dispersed and gathered again—and yet each of us was alone in a way that no previous century had perfected. The crowd was a machine for producing solitude.

And still, beauty ambushed us. A woman's coat the color of arterial red against the gray. A child laughing at pigeons. The way the last light struck the upper floors of the tenements and turned rust into gold. We were not permitted to keep these things. They arrived, they blazed, they vanished, and we carried the afterimage like a wound.

*Strike back*—but against what? The century had no single face. It wore the mask of the state, the mask of the market, the mask of the neighbor who informed on us, the mask of our own tired reflections in the shop windows at dawn. We wanted to rebel, and rebellion was the one thing manufactured in surplus. They sold it back to us in slogans. They printed it on flags and then folded the flags away.

I dreamt of the protests: the human river flooding the boulevards, banners lifted like the sails of some impossible ship. In the dream we were all singing the same song, and the song was old and the song was new, and it said that this time would be different, this time the change would come while it still mattered. In the dream the airplanes turned back. The factories fell silent and let the birds return.

But dreams end, and the waking century went on grinding.

Now I am old, or the century is old, or perhaps we have aged into one another until we cannot be told apart. I look back and I mourn it—yes, even this, even the cruelty, because it was ours, because it was the only life we were given, and it was terrible and it was luminous. We loved fiercely in the ruins. We built our small tenderness in the shadow of the great machines.

And here is the sorrow that outlasts all the others: the reckoning came. The understanding came. The tenderness and the justice and the peace we had been promised—all of it arrived. But it arrived too late. It arrived after the marching feet had stilled, after the last plane had crossed the last sky, after the ones who most deserved to see it had already been folded away like the flags.

*Strike back*, the century murmured at the end, softly now, almost gently, to no one who was left to hear it.

Too late. Too late. And still beautiful. And still ours.

# When New York Comes Alive

There is no city in the world quite like New York, and there is no better way to understand it than to consider *when* it truly comes alive.

**When Morning Breaks**

The first light of day touches the tops of skyscrapers before it reaches the streets below. When New York wakes up, it does so gradually—coffee carts appear on corners, commuters flood the subway stations, and the endless rhythm of the city begins anew. Morning in New York is a promise of possibility.

**When the City Never Sleeps**

New York earned its famous nickname for a reason. When night falls elsewhere, this city only shifts into a different gear. The lights of Times Square blaze against the darkness, restaurants stay open into the early hours, and the streets remain alive with energy. When you visit New York, you quickly learn that time works differently here.

**When Seasons Change**

New York transforms throughout the year. When spring arrives, Central Park bursts into color. When summer heat settles over the boroughs, rooftop gatherings and outdoor concerts fill the calendar. When autumn paints the trees in gold, and when winter dusts the city in snow, New York reveals yet another version of itself.

**When You Belong**

Perhaps the most remarkable thing about New York is that everyone finds their moment. When you least expect it, this city welcomes you as one of its own. Whether you were born here or arrived yesterday, New York has a way of making you feel that you belong.

When people ask what makes New York special, the answer is simple: it is always the right *when*.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem expressing nostalgia and longing for the twentieth century, blending imagery of violence, cities, machines, and delicate natural beauty like peach blossoms.
counterfactuals.output:
# Elegy for a Century That Loved Its Own Wounds

I miss the twentieth century the way a knife misses the throat it never found—that clean nostalgia of almost, that hunger dressed in gabardine.

There were cities then that breathed through iron lungs, exhaling steam and pigeons over boulevards where the electric trams sang their one-note hymns. I remember, or I invent, the way the factories bloomed at dawn, chimneys unfolding their black petals into a sky the color of a healing bruise.

Somewhere a war was always ending. Somewhere a war was always the small print at the bottom of the morning. And still—*still*—the peach trees in the courtyards did not read the newspapers. They opened their pink mouths anyway, obscene with tenderness, dropping their soft artillery onto the cobblestones where the boots had marched and would march again.

O the machines we loved like difficult fathers. The typewriters that stuttered our confessions. The telephones black as revolvers, coiled and waiting to deliver the voice we could not live without. We fed the century our hours and it gave us back the radio, the searchlight, the beautiful and terrible arithmetic of flight.

I am homesick for a violence I can name. For enemies with faces. For the honest smoke.

Come back to me, you decade of broken pianos in the rubble, you afternoon of tanks asleep in the plaza like tired animals, you girl running with a branch of peach blossom held against the fire—petals and cinders indistinguishable now, both drifting, both falling, both trying to tell us something soft about the end.

The century is gone into its own museum. Behind the glass it keeps on burning, keeps on blooming, that impossible orchard planted in the ash, where every spring the dead machines remember they were once, briefly, a kind of music.

And I press my forehead to the cold display and whisper: *take me back to when the world was ending slowly, and there was time enough to watch the blossoms fall.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece in the style of a confessional political prose poem where phrases like "strike back" become the hidden name of an entire century.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Century That Learned to Answer

I.

They told us the century had a face. They lied.
It had a fist, and the fist had a memory,
and the memory was only two words long.

*Strike back.*

Say it slow enough and it becomes a lullaby.
Say it fast enough and it becomes a border.
My grandmother said it in a language
that no longer has a country to be spoken in.

II.

I confess: I loved the symmetry of it.
The clean arithmetic of *you did, so I will.*
I was young and I mistook the echo
for the origin. I thought pain
was a conversation
and not just weather that keeps returning
to the same drowned field.

III.

Every flag I ever pledged to
was a bandage over the same phrase.
Every anthem, when you slow the tape,
becomes those two syllables—
*strike*, the inhale,
*back*, the release—
a breathing exercise for nations
learning to survive their own heartbeat.

IV.

Here is the confession under the confession:
I wanted my enemies to stay enemies.
It was simpler than forgiveness,
which asks you to set down a weight
you have carried so long
it has become the shape of your hands.

I did not know who I was
without the man across the trench,
the ledger, the border, the wound.
We were married, he and I,
by the same two words
whispered from opposite sides of a wall
we both built and called *safety.*

V.

The century signed its name in every treaty
and no one read it,
because it was written in the margins,
in the space between the last shot
and the first apology that came too late.

*Strike back.* The hidden name.
The maiden name of History
before she married the future
and pretended she'd been born innocent.

VI.

So this is my testimony,
spoken into the recorder of no court:

I heard the phrase.
I passed it to my children
the way you pass a coin,
worn smooth by every palm before yours
until the face is gone
and only the round cold weight remains.

And once—just once—
I held it in my mouth
and did not spit it back.

The silence that followed
was the first new word
the century had heard
in a hundred years.

I have no idea what it means yet.

I only know it did not bleed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dreamlike, fragmented monologue about loneliness for a lost era, mixing graffiti, airplanes, bridges, and a protest at the capital.
counterfactuals.output:
They don't build bridges like they used to. I mean the kind you could sleep under, the kind that hummed when the trucks went over, a lullaby of somewhere-else.

There was a word sprayed on the concrete pillar. I forget it now. Something in bubble letters, silver on gray, and it meant *we were here* even after we weren't. The kid who painted it is fifty now, or dead, or an accountant, which is a slower kind of dead.

Airplanes.

I used to count them. Lie flat on the roof tar sticky in July and count the blinking bellies crossing over, red and white, red and white, each one full of people going somewhere they'd complain about later. I never got on. I just liked knowing the sky had a schedule. That someone, somewhere, was expected.

Nobody expects me. That's the fragment I keep tripping over.

At the capital there was a crowd once. Cardboard signs going soft in the rain, everyone's marker running, so all the words wept down into the same gray sentence. We chanted a thing. I can't remember if we won. I remember the back of a stranger's neck, sunburned, and thinking: *I could love a whole country through the back of one neck.* Then the crowd moved and he was gone and that was the closest I ever came.

The bridges. The graffiti. The airplanes stitching the dark.

Here's the trouble with a lost era — you don't know you're inside it until the doors close. You're just living, buying milk, missing buses, and then one day the whole decade is a photograph someone else's mother took, and the colors are wrong, too orange, everyone squinting.

I'm squinting now.

Somewhere under a highway a boy is writing his name in silver so the future will have something to misremember. Somewhere a plane is descending. Somewhere the capital is full of open mouths.

And I am here, which is nowhere in particular, holding the schedule of a sky that no longer lands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem that opens with "I am so lonely for the twentieth century" and moves through themes of reason, machines, and revolt.
counterfactuals.output:
# Elegy for the Machine Age

I am so lonely for the twentieth century, its brass gears and its faith, the way a lever meant *yes* and a switch meant *the world can be divided into on and off*, cleanly, like an egg.

We believed in reason then. Or—no. We *performed* reason, the way one performs a marriage, standing very straight while the machinery of belief turned somewhere behind the walls.

*

Consider the punch card. Consider the beautiful holes we made in things to make them speak. To be legible was to be perforated. To be understood was to be shot through with absence in an ordered way.

I loved the machines because they did not pretend. A piston is honest. A piston says: I will push until I cannot, and then I will push again.

*

But listen—

Beneath the reason there was always the other thing, the red thing, the thing that made the workers put down their tools at exactly 3:14 and walk into the light like people remembering they had bodies.

Revolt is the machine dreaming it is a hand.
Revolt is the equation refusing to balance because it has fallen in love with the wrong side.

*

I am so lonely for the century that thought it was the last one, that carried its wars like heavy furniture up the stairs of history and set them down, exhausted, saying *there, we're finished, we've felt everything now.*

We hadn't.

*

The gears are in museums. The reason has been optimized, distributed, made invisible, made *ambient*—it hums now in rooms without levers, decides without deciding, and there is nothing to push against, no switch, no *no*.

How do you revolt against a fog?

*

So I stand in the twenty-first century holding my obsolete verbs. *To strike. To occupy. To break the loom.* I am so lonely for the enemy who had a face, for the boss you could name, for the whistle that meant *now, together, everyone.*

I am so lonely for the century that still believed a poem could be a wrench thrown into the great turning—

and might, just might,
make the whole magnificent, murderous engine
stop.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, apocalyptic reflection on history and human violence, using tender natural imagery to contrast with the mechanized cruelty of the modern age.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ledger of Ash

The apricot trees do not remember
the names of empires. Each spring
they offer the same white confession
to the indifferent air, petals falling
like a snow that has forgotten winter,
like the small teeth of children
we have buried and unburied
and buried again in the century's slow mouth.

Once there were only stones for killing,
and the hand that threw them
could still be shocked by blood.
Now we have taught iron to think,
have wound the clock of slaughter
so tight it ticks without us—
the drone reciting its arithmetic
over the orchard, over the sleeping village,
over the woman hanging linen
white as surrender in the morning.

I want to tell you about the river.
How it carried, once, only leaves
and the shadows of leaning willows.
How the herons stood in it like clergy,
patient, robed in their own stillness.
And how it carries now the runoff
of our long invention—the ash
that was a library, the ash
that was a face, the ash
that has no name in any tongue
we bothered to keep alive.

*

History is a field we keep on plowing
though we know what surfaces:
the button, the jawbone, the ring
still circling a finger of soil.
We plant our wheat in it regardless.
We have to eat. That is the terrible
tenderness of us—that we grow bread
above the dead and call it morning,
that we let the lilac bloom
against the wall where men were shot
and think the purple beautiful,
and are not wrong, and are not right,
and cannot stop the coming of the season.

*

Let the last testament be simple.
Let it be written in the loosening hand
of someone watching starlings
turn and turn above the ruined station,
that dark cloth thrown across the dusk
and caught before it falls.
We were a species that could build
a wing to hold ten thousand deaths
and could not build a wing
to lift us out of wanting them.

The apricot trees do not remember.
This is their mercy and their judgment.
When the last of us has gone
to feed the roots that do not ask
which uniform, which god, which flag,
the spring will come with its old white silence,
its petals falling on the silent guns,
and no one there to call it grief,
and no one there to call it peace,
and the river going on, and going on,
rinsing the long century from its stones.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
